listings.name: Medina
listings.content: The Medina is the old city quarter located within the sandstone city walls that give Marrakech the nickname the Red City. As an ancient hub, it contains a maze of narrow streets and outdoor marketplaces.

listings.name: Djemaa El-Fna
listings.content: The highlight of any Marrakech night. Musicians, dancers, and story tellers pack this square at the heart of the medina, filling it with a cacophony of drum beats and excited shouts. Scores of stalls sell a wide array of Moroccan fare (see the Eat section) and you will almost certainly be accosted by women wanting to give you a henna tattoo. Amateur boxing matches are sometimes held. Enjoy the various shows, but be prepared to give some dirham to watch or take photos. By day it is largely filled with snake charmers and people with monkeys, as well as some of the more common stalls.

listings.name: The Souks
listings.content: Markets of Marrakech, just adjacent to Place Djemaa El-Fna, are where you can buy almost anything, from spices to shoes, jellabas to kaftans, and tea pots to tagines. Undoubtedly, being a foreigner means you will end up paying higher prices than a native would, but be sure to bargain nonetheless. If you happen to run out of dirham, you will also find plenty of people in the souks who will eagerly exchange your dollars or euros (though a fair rate here is less likely than at an official exchange). All that said, the sellers here are much less aggressive than, say, Egypt, so have fun!

listings.name: Koutoubia Mosque
listings.content: Named after the booksellers market that used to be located here. It is said that the minaret of the Koutoubia mosque is to Marrakech as the Eiffel Tower is to Paris. The minaret is visible from Gueliz which is connected to the Medina by Avenue Mohammed V. At night, the mosque is beautifully lit. The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min founded the first mosque here in 1147 and built the present one beside it in 1158; the excavated remains of the first mosque can be seen on the esplanade next to it. The minaret was completed under Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur (1184 to 1199), and has inspired other buildings such as the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower of Rabat. Non-Muslims are not allowed inside.

listings.name: Tanneries
listings.content: Visiting the tanneries can be an interesting experience. Even if some people tell you the area is only for locals, it is possible to visit the Tanneries without paying a youngster. After finding a tannery, ask one of the workers if you can visit it and take pictures

listings.name: Saadian Tombs
listings.content: Saadian Tombs. The tombs were built in the 16th century as the dynastic necropolis of the Saadian dynasty. The complex includes the Chamber of the Twelve Columns, the Chamber of the Mihrab, the Chamber of the Three Niches and the garden tombs. The site was rediscovered in 1917 and subsequently restored and opened to visitors. The site is relatively compact and most visitors can see the main areas in 20–30 minutes. The Chamber of the Twelve Columns cannot be entered: visitors look in from an opening at its edge, originally a window in the eastern wall, and often have to wait for a turn. The entrance passage is narrow, so arriving early can help avoid queues.
listings.price: Foreigners: adult 100 dirham, children aged 7–13 50 dirham; Moroccan nationals and residents: adult 30 dirham, child 10 dirham

listings.name: Moroccan Culinary Arts Museum
listings.content: If you are interested in food and eating culture, you will enjoy this museum. Audiovisual information about the rich culinary culture of Marocco, its ingredients, techniques and traditions. You can also touch and smell many things. They also sport a very well equipped cooking school.

listings.name: Majorelle Gardens
listings.content: It provides an excellent respite from the hustle and bustle of the city streets, if not crowded by tourists as it sometimes is. The park was designed by the artist Jacques Majorelle in the 1920s and 1930s. Since 1980 the garden has been owned by Yves Saint-Laurent and Pierre Bergé. It boasts a collection of plants from around the globe, including what seems like every cactus species on the planet. Get here early to avoid the crowds. Inside the gardens is also the Berber Museum, which shows a slightly bigger and more modern presentation than the Dar Si Saïd. Advance bookings must be made online, it is not possible to buy a ticket at the site.
listings.price: 170 dirham, 30 dirham extra for the Berber Museum

listings.name: Yves Saint Laurent Museum
listings.content: Advance bookings must be made online, it is not possible to buy a ticket at the site.
listings.price: 120 dirham, combination ticket with Majorelle Gardens and Berber Museum 180 dirham, queues are far shorter here than at the gardens to buy tickets though you have to buy either a YSL Museum ticket or combination ticket

listings.name: Dar Si Saïd Museum
listings.content: Museum set in an old palace with beautiful gardens. While somewhat run-down, it is worth seeing and houses many different artifacts from Morocco through the ages, such as wood carvings, musical instruments, and weapons. It is dedicated to the Moroccan craft industry of wood, gathering a very beautiful collection of popular art: carpets, clothing, pottery and ceramics. All these objects are regional, coming from Marrakech and all the south, especially from Tensift, High Atlas, Soussthe, Anti Atlas, Bani, and Tafilal.
listings.price: Locals: adult 10 dirham, child below 12 3 dirham; tourists: adult 30 dirham

listings.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
listings.content: One of the largest madrassas in North Africa. It is a school attached to the Ben Youssef Mosque and is home to beautiful art and architecture. The present building was completed in 1564–1565 under the Saadian sultan Abdallah al-Ghalib, on the site of an earlier Marinid madrasa. It closed as a school in 1960 and reopened to visitors in 1982. Look for the 11th-century Andalusi marble basin in the prayer hall.
listings.price: Foreigners 50 dirham; Moroccans (with ID) 20 dirham; children under 12 10 dirham

listings.name: El Bahia Palace
listings.content: An ornate palace complex built in the late 19th century, with courtyards, gardens, richly decorated rooms and traditional Moroccan architectural details. The palace was begun in the 1860s by Si Moussa, grand vizier to Sultan Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, and greatly expanded in 1894–1900 by his son Ba Ahmed, Grand Vizier to Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz. The main complex covers almost 2 hectares and has about 150 rooms. The main entrance is on Rue Riad Zitoun el Jedid. The palace is relatively close to other attractions in the southern Medina and can be reached on foot from Jemaa el-Fnaa. Arriving shortly after opening can be useful for visitors who want to avoid the busiest periods.
listings.price: Foreigners: adult 100 dirham, child aged 7–13 50 dirham; Moroccan/resident: adult 30 dirham, child aged 7–13 10 dirham
listings.image: Bahia Palace Marrakech Back Courtyard LL.JPG

listings.name: El Badi Palace
listings.content: The palace complex is extensive, with ruins, courtyards, underground passages and exhibitions. The terrace offers views over the surrounding Medina and the Atlas Mountains on clear days. Allow around 45–90 minutes to explore the main areas. Visitors should check current information before travelling. (updated Aug 2026)
listings.price: Foreigners: adult 100 dirham, child aged 7–13 50 dirham; Moroccan/resident: adult 30 dirham, child aged 7–13 10 dirham

listings.name: The Menara gardens
listings.content: A mixture of orchards and olive groves surrounding the water reservoir with the central pavilion which is a popular sight on tourist postcards. Not a decorative garden, and now quite run down. The pavilion was built during the 16th-century Saadi dynasty, and renovated in 1869. It has a small cafe, but it is not open all hours. There are no toilets open when the cafe is closed.

listings.name: Jewish Cemetery
listings.content: The largest Jewish cemetery in Morocco, characterized by white-washed tombs and sandy graves. The men selling tickets are full of interesting information about the cemetery but you have to ask.

listings.name: Slat Al Azama Synagogue
listings.content: Synagogue which is not only a place of worship with a beautiful open courtyard, but also includes interesting displays about Judaism's varied history in Morocco, including photos of Jews in the Berber Mountains.

listings.name: Marrakech Museum
listings.content: It's housed in the Dar Menebhi Palace, constructed at the end of the 19th century.

listings.name: Musée de la Palmeraie
listings.content: In old agricultural buildings in the Palmeraie, made out of rammed earth. The architecture itself is interesting if you haven't seen it. It offers a small collection of contemporary art, with a room dedicated to Moroccan artists (also famous ones), the international ones are rather not top-notch. The gardens are nicely made and are good place to relax in quiet.

listings.name: Musee Farid Belkahia
listings.content: A museum dedicated to the renowned contemporary artist Farid Belkahia, showcasing different periods of his work

listings.name: Maison de la Photographie
listings.content: A little photography museum, it has one of the highest roof terraces in the Medina. Ticket is also valid for Museum of Mouassin Music.

listings.name: Ali Ben Youssef Mosque
listings.content: The first mosque in Marrakesh was erected at this place by the Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin in the 1070s. However, it was almost completely rebuilt in early 19th century by the Alaouite sultan Suleiman, with hardly any trace left of its original Almoravid or Almohad design. Non-Muslims are not allowed to enter it.

listings.name: Agdal Gardens
listings.content: It consists of groves of orange, lemon, fig, apricot and pomegranate trees in rectangular plots, linked by olive-lined walkways. Together with the medina of Marrakech and the Menara Gardens, the Agdal Gardens were listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1985.

listings.name: Almoravid Koubba
listings.content: A very small but intricate domed pavilion, known for being the only surviving example of Almoravid religious architecture (early 12th century) in Marrakech. Located across the street from the Ben Youssef Mosque, it is believed to have been an annex of the former Almoravid mosque. It was excavated in the 20th century after being half-buried for centuries. The pavilion's exterior can be easily seen from the street, so paying for entry just lets you see its interior.

listings.name: Chez Ali Fantasia
listings.content: Horse show, acrobats on Arabian horses firing rifles in the air, horseback acrobatics, belly dancing, etc. It takes place at night in a huge imitation of an old castle.

listings.name: Stade de Marrakesh
listings.content: This is multi-use but mostly for football, with a capacity of 41,356. It's the home ground of Kawkab, who play in Botola 2 the second tier. In 2025 / 26 it hosted matches in the Africa Cup of Nations.

listings.name: Marrakech Paragliding
listings.content: Leave the city behind and discover the incredible beauty of Morocco from above! Enjoy an exciting tandem paragliding experience near Marrakech, surrounded by the spectacular Atlas Mountains.

listings.name: Moratra Medina walking tour
listings.content: A 2- to 4-hour walk through the old city with a licensed local guide, covering how the souks and their crafts are organised and landmarks such as the Bahia Palace, Ben Youssef Madrasa and the Saadian Tombs.
listings.price: US$20 per person in a small group, US$60 per person private

listings.name: Les Bains de Marrakech
listings.content: Tourists-oriented in good sense: couples can have hammam together in a private room. Extensive list of massages and spa treatments from 30 min to a full day. Reception and attendants are proficient in speaking English, however, the scrubbing and massage personnel speak only very basic vocabulary. You need to book two days in advance.
listings.address: 2 Derb Sedra, Bab Agnaou (same building as Riad Mehdi)

listings.name: Thai marrakech
listings.content: Bann Thai institute is a beauty center based in the heart of Marrakech. His team is a graduate of the famous school of Wat Po in Bangkok. The center offers several Thai massage relaxation with a traditional Moroccan hammam natural products
listings.address: Résidence Les Jasmins Apt N° 13 4ème étage Angle Av. Mohamed v et Rue Oum Errabia Guéliz

listings.name: Hamam Essalama
listings.content: Friendly staff, however, no English or French (other locals helped without any problem)

listings.name: Ô Bain de Lina
listings.content: Friendly staff, however, no English or French; other customers likely to help you out.
listings.address: N 1, 84 Avenue Hassan II Residence El Faroukia

listings.name: Chez Chegrouni
listings.content: Their vegetarian couscous is supposedly the only true vegetarian couscous in town; it's also bland but they give you plenty of it. Prices go up if you sit on the terrace. Usually packed full of good-time tourists.

listings.name: Chez Yassine
listings.content: Not much choice but served by very friendly people. Tajines and pizzas are great and you can also order skewers that are not on the menu.

listings.name: Henna Cafe
listings.content: A pretty little cafe on 3 floors with an orange sign on the Berber hand-carved wooden facade opened in November 2011. You can have a cup of tea or coffee or simple lunch with dessert or just a sandwich. The Henna Café offers safe henna body adornment as well-ranging from a 50 dirham small motif on your hand to a full arm complex design for a wedding from 500 dirham. All profits go to local causes. Henna cafe was set up by the owners of Riad Cinnamon and Riad Papillon and Vivid Trading in order to start to 'give back' to Marrakech and offer support to those who might want it. The café offers free English lessons to Moroccan women so that they can find employment out of the home.

listings.name: Chez Bismilah
listings.content: Amazing food and wonderful service. The owner is very kind and the fantastic chef is a humble lady who cooks perfectly all the traditional Moroccan recipes. Tayine Royale is recommended. The roof top has an amazing view over the old medina.

listings.name: Café Babouche medina
listings.content: In a small street a few steps from the Jemaa El Fna square. You can eat there in a friendly atmosphere. The veal tagine with prunes and almonds is spectacular.

listings.name: Black Pan
listings.content: Italian restaurant. Artisanal pizzas, traditional Italian dishes and warm atmosphere.

listings.name: Associacion Amal
listings.content: Here you can experience lunch similar to what Moroccans eat at home: this women's aid association provides women with education in exchange for food which is then sold for financing the model.

listings.name: 16 Café
listings.content: Moroccan kitchen. 16 café is caterer of events and weddings.

listings.name: Café Arabe
listings.content: They have a Moroccan and an Italian cook, so there are two menus to choose from. There are three floors including the downstairs courtyard which is lovely for lunch. The top floor terrace has fantastic views, you can lounge on their sofas sipping a cocktail and watching the sun go down over the medina.

listings.name: sky mabrouka
listings.content: Serves the same standard fare as everywhere else in a little courtyard or terrace.

listings.name: Al Fassia
listings.content: Traditional Moroccan food in cozy restaurant run by women (except the doorman). Wine served by the bottle.

listings.name: Café du Livre
listings.content: A western style bookshop-café in the villa nouvelle

listings.name: Café Kabash
listings.content: Have a roof terrace with a good view. Daily Moroccan menus with tea and juice.

listings.name: Le Marrakchi
listings.content: With two main courses and wine running at around 300 dirham, this is one of the poshest restaurants in the square. The food is not necessarily better than elsewhere, but it is one of the few restaurants that serves alcohol. It also has a completely enclosed upstairs terrace, which is ideal for views of the square when the weather is bad.
listings.address: Place jeema el-fna, 52 Rue des Banques

listings.name: Le Bistrot Loft
listings.content: Steaks, bistro food and good wines. Bar with beer, aperitifs and cocktails.

listings.name: Diaffa
listings.content: An upscale restaurant in one of the oldest buildings in the Medina, and offers Moroccan cuisine in an ambiance that recalls the Orient at the height of its magic and glory. The food, building (whether the tables around the central courtyard and fountain or the second-level balcony), and tactful and tasteful entertainment.

listings.name: Dar Najat's Kitchen
listings.content: Daily fresh food in a boutique riad.
listings.address: Douar Groua, derb lalla chacha, N.18

listings.name: Maison de la Photographie
listings.content: A little photography museum, it has one of the highest roof terraces in the Medina. Over lunch of a fixed-price menu (at 75 dirham as of 2012) you get panoramic views over the city and the High Atlas mountains.

listings.name: Pepe Nero
listings.content: Fine Italian and Moroccan dining in gorgeous Riad. Often full so make a reservation.
listings.price: 400 dirham for 3-4 course dinner, wine for 200 dirham

listings.name: La Villa des Orangers
listings.content: French gastronomic cuisine in a very calm and pleasant atmosphere. Enjoy your dinner in soft chairs, among dark woodpanels, bookcases and artwork. In the winter start with a drink at the fireplace.
listings.price: 700 dirham for three-course menu. 500 dirham for a bottle of wine.

listings.name: Le Grand Café de la Poste
listings.content: French brasserie with Moroccan influence in the former post office.
listings.address: Boulevard El mansour Eddahbi and Avenue Imam Malik

listings.name: Le Grand Salon
listings.content: Upscale restaurant with French cuisine. Serve organic vegetables and olive oil from its own gardens.

listings.name: Dar Yacout
listings.content: Traditional Moroccan gastronomic cuisine. Has a terrace overlooking the Medina.
listings.address: 79, derb Sidi Ahmed Soussi, Bab Doukkala

listings.name: Le Foundouk
listings.content: Moroccan and European cuisine. Roof terrace and bar.

listings.name: Les Jardins de la Medina
listings.content: Traditional and modern Moroccan cuisine. Moroccan wine served by bottle and glass. Stylish restaurant with tall white columns.

listings.name: Eloomm
listings.content: Mediterranean restaurant where slow dining meets Moroccan produce.

listings.name: Chesterfield Pub
listings.content: A slightly unusual experience, apparently an 'English pub' it serves Moroccan lager and has an outside pool in a courtyard with palm trees, not an entirely English experience. Much less touristy than it sounds with a mainly local clientele. It serves a decent pint.

listings.name: Le Salama
listings.content: Happy hour from 17:00 until they close, mostly western pop classics on the top floor. Very touristy with shishas, belly dancing and waiters who wear a fez - none of it is typically Moroccan but the overall atmosphere is between relaxed and party vibe. Also offers traditional Moroccan snacks. Good for smaller (up to 10 people) groups.

listings.name: Hotel Grand Tazi
listings.content: The hotel has a public bar, serving beer and wine and is not overly expensive.

listings.name: Narwama
listings.content: Restaurant and bar that has a fire fountain in the centre and an open roof around the patio. The atmosphere is very chilled and their food is very good, but slightly expensive. Good for pre-dinner drinks.

listings.name: Montecristo
listings.content: Nightclub with rooftop terrace

listings.name: Jad Mahal
listings.content: Lounge bar and formal restaurant.

listings.name: Sky Lounge
listings.content: Fashionable rooftop lounge on top of the Pearl Hotel

listings.name: Comptoir Darna
listings.content: Cocktail bar and night club Dress code: elegant

listings.name: African Chic
listings.content: Moroccan Latin Brazilian. Also has a restaurant with a view to the dance floor.

listings.name: Dar Attajmil
listings.content: Centrally located and easy to reach, Dar Attajmil has a sand colored courtyard shaded by a tall banana tree; 4 double rooms with bathroom, 1 family suite with private courtyard, several cozy sitting areas, fireplace and library, a large terrace garden where breakfast and meals are served and a devoted team of 5 lovely persons; hammam, massages, cooking class available. Owner organic farm near Essaouira provides daily fresh products, olive and argan oil and the opportunity to spend one or more days in this old restored property, among the argan trees.

listings.name: Dar Jaguar
listings.content: Dar Jaguar is an ancient riad that has been restored as a beautiful private guesthouse. It is situated in the heart of the old medina, neighbouring the exotic Place des Epices (spice market).
listings.address: 7-8 Derb El Mesfioui, Rahba Kedima, Medina

listings.name: Riad Abaka
listings.content: A spacious riad with seven beautifully furnished bedrooms and ensuite bathrooms.

listings.name: Riad Amazigh
listings.content: A former luxury riad, now a beautiful hostel. Doubles, singles, and dorms which house up to 8 people. Roof top terrace with nice views, unheated pool, restaurant and bar. Wi-Fi in communal areas, breakfast included. Open 24 hrs, can book activities and excursions.

listings.name: Riad Basma
listings.content: 5 double rooms with bathroom.

listings.name: Riad Chennaoui
listings.content: Simple and basic riad in the Medina. The staff are friendly and happy to discuss Moroccan life and culture over a shisha in the evening. This place can be difficult to find – you may have to pay a local to take you there (10–20 dirham should do it, although they will ask for more).
listings.address: Riad Zitoune Jdid, Derb Sidi Fares N°01

listings.name: Riad Cinnamon
listings.content: Designed and rebuilt to a very high standard with attention to detail. Unexpected extras such as the loan of a local mobile phone and ipad. Dinners served on roof terrace with nice views, pools on patio and roof garden terrace. 5 rooms that can accommodate 3 to 4 people each, with an overall maximum of 16.

listings.name: Riad Dar Eliane
listings.content: Four spacious double bedrooms and bathrooms with A/C. Accommodation is on two floors of a restored 300 year old riad in an older quarter of Marrakesh. Ten minute walk to Jamaa el Fna.

listings.name: Riad Iaazane
listings.content: A restored riad with extensive use of traditional styling and ceramics, includes a roof terrace with views. Shower, internet with Wi-Fi access, washing, shisha (hooka), free mint tea, city map. An authentic local style breakfast included (08:30–11:30). The owners also operate a tour company that offers guided and structured tours of 1–3 days.

listings.name: Riad LakLak
listings.content: A riad built in the 17th century, which sleeps 12 in 2 suites and 3 bedrooms, that can be rented as a whole.

listings.name: Riad Laksiba
listings.content: £25-30 per person depending on season. A very popular Riad with UK visitors. Five bedrooms all with bespoke hand carved beds designed to be split to make twin bedrooms. From Bab Ksiba, an entrance into the Royal Kasbah quarter of the Medina, 1st right is Derb Kadi and Riad Laksiba is the last house in this little cul-de-sac. Ten minute walk to the Djemaa el-Fna main square.

listings.name: Riad Lotus Perle
listings.content: Riad Lotus Perle is in the Medina, in an old neighborhood near the lively souks and Djemaa El-Fna square, this is a wonderful riad composed of rooms and suites combining authenticity and modernity.

listings.name: Riad Magellan
listings.content: An elegant six-bedroom riad which offers a restful and relaxing atmosphere, in the Mouassine district. Traditional Moroccan meals are available as well as complementary Wi-Fi internet. Airport transfer service available on request.

listings.name: Riad Melhoun
listings.content: Located in central Marrakech, a 3-minute walk from the El Badi and El Bahia Palaces, it features an interior courtyard with a swimming pool and a furnished rooftop terrace with views of the medina. Each room has traditional Moroccan decoration and en-suite shower. Guests also have access to a traditional living room with a fireplace and a lounge area with books. Free Wi-Fi is available in common areas, hammam, massages and traditional meals are provided on request.
listings.address: 99 Derb Sidi Moussa, Quartier de la Bahia, 40007 Marrakech Médina

listings.name: Riad Naila
listings.content: Riad Naila Marrakech is a gorgeous private rental home in the Medina of Marrakech built around a patio with a large roof terrace. It is in the Medina of Marrakech in a calm area a fifteen-minute walk away from the Djemaa El-Fna square. It has four bedrooms which sleep seven persons. Each bedroom has its own bath room. Additionally are available a fully equipped kitchen, a Moroccan lounge and a library.
listings.price: Riad Naila Marrakech is a private rental home. Prices range from €100-140 per day depending on the season for the entire house (sleeps 7 persons)
listings.address: Marrakech Medina, Mosquée Sidi Ben Slimane

listings.name: Riad Dar Najat
listings.content: Jacuzzi on the roof terrace, Wi-Fi throughout the riad, 7 ensuite shower and A/C accommodation with great gastronomy. French owner, friendly team and atmosphere.
listings.address: Douar Graoua, Derb Lalla Chacha, No.18

listings.name: Riad Papillon
listings.content: A riad with five beautiful rooms: Rose, Jasmine, Bougainvillea, Hibiscus and Geranium. It is located in the heart of the Dar el Basha antique district which is very safe. Cuisine is exceptional, service is warm and attentive but discrete. Papillon offers loan of local phone/iPad, IPhone charger, bathrobes. Breakfast and Wi-Fi internet are included. Very romantic and wonderful atmosphere with welcoming dipping pool and tent on roof terrace. Airport pickups available.
listings.price: Rooms range from £50-100 according to the season. Ask about any special offers and last minute deals

listings.name: Hotel Riad Primavera
listings.content: The only kosher hotel in all of Morocco. The kosher certification is in the lobby and is issued by the Beth Din of Marrakech. 22 rooms with personal A/C units, TVs, bathrooms with showers, decorated in typical Moroccan style. Prices tend to rise during major Jewish holidays and festivals.

listings.name: Riad Dar Zaman
listings.content: A gorgeous old riad with four en suite rooms, in the historic Sidi Ben Slimane district. Cuisine is exquisite, service is warm and attentive, price includes breakfast, designer toiletries, mint tea and pastries and Wi-Fi internet. Fantastic views of Atlas Mountains from roof terrace, deliciously refreshing dipping pool, wonderful dreamy atmosphere.
listings.price: Rooms range from £50-100 according to the season. Askfor special offers and last minute deals.

listings.name: Riad Zara
listings.content: Run by the friendly and helpful owner Monique and her assistant Hassan. Features a rooftop terrace with nice views of Medina and cozy cane chairs, and a small pool in the center of the Riad. Traditional meals such as Tajines can be served any time of the day. Breakfast includes an array of jams, amlou, pancakes, and mint tea and can be served at flexible times. In the evening, candles are lit and guests gather around the pool, enjoying wine and if you're lucky Hassan might give a live music performance.

listings.name: Riad Zolah
listings.content: Chic while cozy and informal riad run by Ismail and his team. The house cook, Fadila, makes fabulous fresh baked breads at breakfast. Gorgeous roof terrace and two candle-lit/petal-strewn courtyard patios (one with plunge pool).

listings.name: Ryad Dyor
listings.content: Riad hotel with 7 luxury suites.

listings.name: Riad Al Loune
listings.content: Charming Riad with pool and hammam.

listings.name: Hotel Ali
listings.content: Rue Moulay Ismail. Beds in en suite, dorms, and rooftop terrace mattresses for 60 dirham per person per night, including cooked breakfasts served with orange juice and fresh coffee. Dorm guests can use the internet cafe for 5 dirham per hour. They have a laundry service and free internet access for private room guests, money exchange, a terrace restaurant with views of Djemaa El-Fna, and a downstairs hammam. Private rooms are available with a maximum per person price of 250 dirham per night including breakfast, free internet, and a daily traditional Hammam.

listings.name: Hotel Salam (laksor)
listings.content: Cheap and clean hotels, doesn't seem to have showers.
listings.price: 100 dirham for double room, no bathroom
listings.address: bab ftouh rue haram chikh n.14, laksor, marrakech

listings.name: Hotel Atlas
listings.content: 50 Derb Sidi Bouloukat. A 2-min walk to the famous square of Djemaa El-Fna. Clean and friendly with nice rooms with shared bathrooms. Singles from 90 dirham, doubles from 170 dirham, for 3 people 250 dirham, for 4 people 280 dirham, for 5 people 320 dirham. There are some rooms with AC for an additional 50 dirham. The hotel is charming and all arranged in the traditional way.

listings.name: Hotel Central Palace
listings.content: Rooms are around a noisy and echoey central courtyard. Rooms are clean, but the shared toilets can be another story. Indifferent staff and housekeepers. Nice terrace with a great view, and rooms starting at 150 dirham for a double room with shared showers and toilet. You get what you pay for, but all in all it's a good value considering that Marrakech is more expensive that most other places in Morocco. Car rentals can be arranged (around 350 dirham per day for a small but fairly new car).

listings.name: Hotel el-Ward
listings.content: Clean, quite comfortable, and the owners are very friendly whenever they feel like it. The rooftop terrace isn't lavish, but being one of the highest it does have a great view. 60/120/170/220 dirham for single/double/triple/quadruple.

listings.name: Hotel Essaouira
listings.content: The hotel has singles with a shared bath from 50 dirham and doubles from 90 dirham. It is more or less like the others, but it's all painted in the traditional way, which gives it charm. Toilets and showers are bare-bones, a norm at this price range. Hot water does not stay hot for long. Overall a very good value and comfortable place from which to explore the old town.

listings.name: Hotel Imouzzer
listings.content: One of the cheapest and best-value hotels with rooms starting at 65 dirham for singles and 120 dirham for doubles (slightly higher in high season), all with shared bathrooms. Rooms are arranged around a traditional courtyard, and both rooms and shared bathrooms are clean with hot water. The hotel also has a comfortable terrace where you can eat breakfast for 20 dirham.

listings.name: Hotel Sindi
listings.content: Sud 109, Derb Sidi Bouloukat, Riad Zitoun El Kidim,

listings.name: Hotel Smara
listings.content: Very clean, friendly people, nice rooms. 50 dirham and doubles 80 dirham.

listings.name: Hotel Cecil
listings.content: At the Djemaa El-Fna, Bouloukate. Offers doorms, rooms with shared bathroom (from US$13 per person), and ensuite rooms with AC (from US$18 per person). Rooftop breakfast and Wi-Fi included.

listings.name: Palm Plaza Hotel and Spa
listings.content: . Luxurious and comfortable providing 230 rooms, including 151 twin, 52 double, 2 rooms for disabled persons, 6 junior suites, 20 senior suites and a royal suite. The hotel has a piano bar, night club and a restaurant. Snacks are available at the pool bar. The spa features a heated indoor swimming pool, a sauna, a hammam and a gym.
listings.address: Avenue du 7ieme Art Zone Touristique Agdal

listings.name: Riad Lyla
listings.content: In Laksour district, 2 min from Djemaa El-Fna, Lyla Riad Marrakech opens its doors. Gérard is the riad's passionate owner.

listings.name: Riad Rahba
listings.content: Offers private, en suite rooms and is a minute from Djemaa El-Fna, at the entrance to the Souks. The Riad combines the traditional Moroccan atmosphere with the comforts of a modern hostel and hotel. The rates include breakfast and wifi. From €18 per single en suite room per night.

listings.name: Le Vizir Center Park Resort
listings.content: Suites decorated in 3 different styles of architecture.
listings.address: Route de Casablanca, Ouled ben Rahmoun

listings.name: Marrakech Rose
listings.content: Charming little hostel right in the center of town, with small dorms and super-friendly staff. Great place to meet other travellers and socialize - mostly a younger crowd. Not the best choice if you want an early night's sleep.
listings.address: 13 Derb Laadam, Kenaria, Place Jemaa el Fna

listings.name: Massine II
listings.content: 2nd backpackers in Marrakech in the old Medina. Originally a 16th century house. Central garden, and rooftop. Shower, internet, washing facilities. Breakfast is available, book early, this is a popular establishment. Some travellers complain the sheets are not changed regularly. Also, travellers aren't always registered properly.

listings.name: The Heart of the Medina backpackers hostel
listings.content: 1st backpackers hostel to be located in the Medina. 1 minute walk from Place Djemaa El-Fna. Rooftop terrace, hot showers, comfortable surroundings. No more than 6 beds to a room. Breakfast included as are bed linens, towels, and free Wi-Fi. You can expect to pay €8/person all year round per night if booked in advance via email or website. No lockouts, no curfews, and is open 24/7, 365 days/ year.

listings.name: Rue Mohammed el-Hansali
listings.content: A clean hostel with a 23:30 curfew and obligatory wake up call at 08:00. Daily daytime lockout. It is a fair distance from the action in the heart of the Medina. A taxi can cost 15-20 dirham.

listings.name: Sirayane boutique hotel & spa
listings.content: Spread across nearly 5 acres of gardens, this boutique hotel faces the Atlas Mountains.

listings.name: Hotel Toulousain
listings.content: A budget-friendly hotel with rooms going off two nice courtyards, located in a rear building and therefore quiet, no luxury equipment but clean, tidy and friendly and helpful staff
listings.price: 150 dirham per night for a single room without bathroom up to 600 dirham double room 'Suite Hotel', breakfast included

listings.name: Hotel al Kabir
listings.content: This modern, airy hotel is one of a group of similar standard hotels in this area of Guéliz. Mainly used by tour groups and reservation agencies, the Hotel al Kabir's rooms, accessible from three elevators, are all clean, modern, and well appointed, if a tad sterile, and the bathrooms are a reasonable size with shower/tub combos.

listings.name: La Mamounia
listings.content: Conceived in 1923 by architects Henri Prost and Antoine Marchisio, the hotel opened in 1929, combining Moroccan architecture with the Art Deco style. Renovated in 2009 and 2020. The hotel includes a 10-ha garden, colonnaded courtyards, terraces, swimming pools, a spa, and a health club in a glass cube. Many celebrities have stayed at the hotel, including Winston Churchill, Nelson Mandela, Paul MacCartney and Andy Warhol.

listings.name: Hotel Ibis
listings.content: A more impersonal European chain hotel, but very clean and peaceful. It is within a short taxi ride of all the action. If you want to be able to escape the hustle and bustle during the heat of the day and chill out by a pool, this place is perfect. Decent value for the money as well, with lovely rooms and showers. Free internet with wifi is provided in the lobby.

listings.name: Moroccan House Hotel
listings.content: A colorful and personable hotel. As the name suggests, this is more like a house than a standard block hotel. The extravagantly painted and decorated interior is entered through bright blue heavy wood studded doors. Choice of various brightly colored interiors furnished with faux-antiques and lace-draped four-poster beds. Each bathroom has its own water heater and bath/shower combo, and comes supplied with a range of toiletries. Close to many of Guéliz's better restaurants and shops.
listings.price: 3-star rooms start at 405 dirham single, 484 dirham double; 4-star Pacha suites: 455 dirham single, 624 dirham double; 5-star Prince suites: 527 dirham single, 764 dirham double.

listings.name: Oudaya Hotel
listings.content: Situated close to the railway station, the Oudaya is a good alternative for travellers looking for a medium prized hotel in the Ville Nouvelle. The rooms are clean and well-kept with good size bathrooms, air-condition and TV. Breakfast is served from early in the morning and consists of a well stocked buffet, the restaurant is however mediocre and much better meals can be had just around the corner. The courtyard has a large pool (open 09:00-18:00) lined with a massive bougainvilla. The hotel does have a policy of no outside food, which includes bottled water, so make sure to keep any purchases hidden when entering.

listings.name: Villa Dar El Kanoun
listings.content: Route de Targa. Luxury B&B villa with swimming pool and garden. It offers five comfortable double rooms in a quiet residential area nearby Marrakech downtown. Breakfast is included. Rates begin at 1,000 dirham for a double room.

places.title: Bahia Palace

places.title: El Badi Palace

places.title: Dar el Bacha
places.blurb: Dar el Bacha is a palace situated in the old medina of Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Ben Youssef Mosque
places.blurb: The Ben Youssef Mosque or Ibn Yusuf Mosque, is a mosque in the Medina quarter of Marrakesh, Morocco, named after the Almoravid ruler Ali ibn Yusuf.

places.title: Almoravid Qubba
places.blurb: The Almoravid Qubba, also known as the Qubbat al-Ba'diyyin or Qubbat al-Barudiyyin, is a small monument in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Agdal Gardens
places.blurb: The Agdal Gardens are a large area of historic gardens and orchards in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Kasbah Mosque, Marrakesh
places.blurb: The Kasbah Mosque, also known as the Moulay al-Yazid Mosque, is a historic mosque in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Dar Si Said
places.blurb: Dar Si Said is a historic late 19th-century palace and present-day museum in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Bab Doukkala Mosque
places.blurb: The Bab Doukkala Mosque or Mosque of Bab Doukkala is a mosque in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Ben Salah Mosque
places.blurb: The Ben Salah Mosque or Ben Saleh Mosque is a 14th-century mosque in the historic medina of Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Barrima Mosque
places.blurb: The Barrima Mosque is a mosque in Marrakesh, Morocco, attached to the Kasbah and Royal Palace of the city.

places.title: Majorelle Garden
places.blurb: The Majorelle Garden is a one-hectare botanical garden and artist's landscape garden in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Marrakech Museum
places.blurb: The Museum of Marrakech is a historic palace and museum located in the old center of Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Menara Gardens
places.blurb: The Menara Gardens are a historic public garden and orchard in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Yamama, Morocco
places.blurb: Yamama is a northern neighborhood of Marrakesh in the Marrakesh-Safi region of Morocco.

places.title: Shrob ou Shouf Fountain
places.blurb: The Shrob ou Shouf Fountain or Chrob ou Chouf Fountain is a historic wall fountain in the medina of Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakesh
places.blurb: The Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech is a museum dedicated to the fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent located in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Mouassine Museum
places.blurb: The Mouassine Museum is a museum in the Mouassine neighbourhood of the historic medina of Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Oued Tensift Bridge
places.blurb: The Oued Tensift Bridge is a historic bridge over the Tensift River located just north of Marrakesh in Morocco.

places.title: Mouassine Fountain
places.blurb: The Mouassine Fountain is a part of the 16th-century religious complex of the Mouassine Mosque in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Marrakesh Stadium
places.blurb: The Marrakesh Stadium is a multi-use stadium in Marrakesh, Morocco.

places.title: Museum of African Contemporary Art Al Maaden
places.blurb: The Museum of African Contemporary Art Al Maaden or MACAAL, is an independent, nonprofit museum of contemporary art in Marrakesh, Morocco.
